title: Large-Scale Comparison of Metaheuristic Algorithms via Behavioral Verification of Large Language Model–Generated Codes
authors: Alharbi Emad
abstract: The performance and reproducibility of metaheuristic algorithms remain unresolved because prior studies have examined only limited subsets, as most algorithms are published as mathematical descriptions without source code. A large language model (LLM) was used to implement 393 published metaheuristic algorithms. The LLM-generated codes were verified by running it on two optimization problems with three seeds while an automated script checked for crashes and improvement. These reports were returned to the LLM as repair feedback. First drafts passed at a rate of 53.4%, which increased to 78.4% after eight rounds of feedback, while 32 algorithms failed identically across all runs. The common practice of using LLMs to review LLM-generated code was evaluated: two independent LLM reviewers approved 75% of broken codes, indicating that textual review provides no information about functional correctness. Fifty verified codes were compared to reference codes from an established library: 49 differed significantly in both directions, and only the most completely specified algorithm was equivalent. The 360 verified codes were compared on the Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) 2017 and CEC 2022 benchmarks with 51 seeded runs. Classical Differential Evolution ranked second on CEC 2017 and first on CEC 2022, outperforming hundreds of more recent metaphor-based algorithms.

title: Large Language Model-Assisted Safe Translation of Ambiguous Power Dispatch Language into Precise Machine Instructions
authors: 张 佳豪; Jianzhou Feng; Wang Xiaohuan
abstract: Increasing renewable penetration and operational complexity make dispatch instructions difficult to execute when they contain ambiguous topological references, incomplete parameters, and implicit safety requirements. This study develops a large language model (LLM)-assisted framework that translates ambiguous power-dispatch language into precise machine instructions. The AI contribution is a constrained language-understanding architecture that combines dynamic intent routing and task-adaptive slot filling with topology-aware entity grounding, safety verification, and deterministic domain-specific-language compilation. The engineering application is a verifiable interface between dispatchers&apos; natural-language instructions and power-system control operations: targets are grounded in IEEE33, IEEE69, and IEEE118 topology semantic profiles, while unsafe or incomplete requests are rejected or returned for clarification. A bilingual Chinese-English dataset is constructed to evaluate the framework. Across single- and multi-topology settings, the method achieves high domain-specific-language matching and end-to-end success rates; ablation studies show the contributions of routing, task-adaptive schemas, grounding, and safety rejection. The framework supports structured, executable, and auditable power-dispatch interaction without allowing a generative model to issue control commands directly.

title: Multidimensional Evaluation of Large Language Models on the AAP In-Service Examination: Assessing Accuracy, Calibration, and Citation Reliability
authors: Dhaimade Prita Abhay; Henderson Robin
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Background
                  Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated rapid advancements in natural language understanding and generation, prompting their integration into biomedical research, clinical practice, and professional education. However, systematic evaluation of LLMs in specialty-specific domains such as dentistry and periodontology remain limited, particularly regarding multidimensional performance metrics.
                
                
                  Objective
                  To conduct a comprehensive, multidimensional assessment of commercially available LLMs: GPT-4.0, GPT-5.0, and Claude SONNET 4.0 on the American Academy of Periodontology in-service examination, focusing on response accuracy, self-assessed confidence calibration, citation validity, and hallucination prevalence.
                
                
                  Methods
                  Models were evaluated on the 2024 AAP In-Service Examination (331 questions) using two formats: Full Test (all questions at once) and Individual Question (one at a time). Prompts were standardized; models selected answers, and for GPT-5.0 and Claude SONNET 4.0, also provided confidence ratings and citations. Citation validity was assessed using a human-in-the-loop protocol with expert review. Statistical analyses included chi-square, McNemar’s, and logistic regression to assess accuracy, question fatigue, confidence calibration, and citation reliability.
                
                
                  Results
                  LLMs achieved high overall accuracy (78–87%), with the Individual Question format consistently yielding higher scores than Full Test, though differences were not statistically significant.
                  Accuracy was highest in fact-dense domains (biochemistry, physiology, microbiology) and lowest in integrative domains (diagnosis, therapy). Significant question fatigue was observed in GPT-5.0 Full Test mode (OR = 0.997, p = 0.035), but not in Individual Question mode.
                  Confidence scores predicted accuracy, with the strongest calibration in Individual Question mode. Citation analysis revealed frequent hallucinations, mostly critically erroneous, and citation validity was independent of answer accuracy.
                
                
                  Conclusions
                  LLMs can answer a broad spectrum of periodontal specialty questions, but their reliability varies with context and information presentation. While promising as adjunctive tools, their outputs— especially for complex reasoning and citations—require rigorous human review in educational and research settings to ensure accuracy and safety.
                
                
                  Author Summary
                  Artificial intelligence chatbots are rapidly entering medical education, yet we lack comprehensive understanding of their reliability when students depend on them for learning. We developed a multidimensional evaluation framework to systematically assess AI performance beyond simple accuracy, examining how these systems behave across different medical topics, question types, and presentation formats.
                  Using 331 real dental examination questions, we tested three major AI systems, analyzing not only correctness but also confidence calibration - whether AI confidence levels match actual accuracy - and implementing human-in-the-loop verification to check if cited sources actually exist.
                  Our findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in current AI systems. Most alarmingly, these chatbots fabricated nearly half of their citations while maintaining unwavering confidence in both correct and incorrect responses. This combination of overconfidence and misinformation means students cannot distinguish reliable from unreliable AI responses. Additionally, we documented progressive performance decline during sequential questioning, similar to human cognitive fatigue.
                  While we know AI systems generate rather than retrieve information, our research demonstrates the real-world consequences of this limitation. As artificial intelligence integrates into education, healthcare diagnostics, and insurance decisions, these findings underscore the urgent need for better evaluation frameworks and user education about AI limitations.

title: Large Language Model Automated Construction of Continuous-Adjoint Topology Optimization Solvers
authors: Yu Xinyi; Qian Xiaoping
abstract: Continuous-adjoint topology optimization (TO) relies on explicit adjoint equations and design sensitivities that must be re-derived when the governing equations, objective, constraints, or optimization variable change. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific continuous adjoints, verification code, and complete TO code, reducing the required manual work. Three target files specify the formulation, verification, and optimization. Structural TO and fluid TO reference packages connect the formulation and derivation to adjoint-field and sensitivity checks and the TO loop. The LLM first writes a derivation containing the target residual, continuous-adjoint equations, and sensitivities. It then generates verification code comparing implemented adjoint fields with adjoints from the transposed residual Jacobian and sensitivities from automatic differentiation. Only code passing both checks is used to generate the complete TO code. Across six problems, four LLM configurations, and two reference packages, the verification gate admitted 31 of 48 combinations; all 31 produced a complete TO code passing the final checks within three Step~3 generations, and 82 of 93 Step~3 codes passed. In these problems, the conjugate heat-transfer case retained coupled velocity--pressure--temperature adjoints and sensitivities. Without a target interface-filtering structural optimization implementation, the LLM generated and checked its adjoint filter equation, sensitivities with respect to \(R_{\mathrm{eff}}\), and a complete solver with prescribed \(\gamma_{\mathrm{seed}}\) updates. By relying on reusable instructions and references and independent checks, the LLM automates continuous-adjoint TO solver construction for new formulations, from problem-specific derivation to complete TO code.

title: Model Distillation Techniques for Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in Mobile AI Tools
authors: Podolski Jeffery
abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile and edge devices remains fundamentally constrained by the tension between model capability and hardware feasibility. While multi-billion-parameter models achieve remarkable performance across natural language tasks, their memory footprint, inference latency, and energy consumption far exceed what smartphones and embedded systems can sustain. Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a primary technique for compressing LLMs into compact student models suitable for on-device deployment, yet significant challenges persist in transferring reasoning capabilities, preserving safety alignment, and optimizing for heterogeneous mobile hardware. This paper presents a systematic review and analysis of model distillation techniques specifically for deploying LLMs in mobile AI tools. We examine the methodological landscape across white-box approaches (logit-based distillation, reverse KL divergence, layer-wise hint transfer) and black-box techniques (chain-of-thought distillation, instruction-following transfer, context distillation), alongside complementary compression strategies including quantization and pruning. Through analysis of empirical results from recent benchmarks, we identify a three-way trade-off between model compression, response quality, and latency that governs deployment feasibility on mobile-class hardware. Our findings indicate that hybrid distillation pipelines combining knowledge transfer with activation-aware quantization enable sub-billion-parameter models to achieve sub-500ms response latency on CPU platforms, while preserving approximately 85-90% of teacher model accuracy on domain-specific tasks. We further analyze open challenges including vocabulary mismatch in cross-architecture distillation, error compounding in autoregressive student models, safety preservation under aggressive compression, and the lack of standardized evaluation frameworks for mobile LLM deployment. This review provides a structured reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to navigate the design space between model capability and mobile deployment constraints.

title: Accuracy of Prospective Assessments of 4 Large Language Model Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions About Emergency Care: Experimental Comparative Study (Preprint)
authors: Yau Jonathan Yi-Shin; Saadat Soheil; Hsu Edmund; Murphy Linda Suk-Ling; Roh Jennifer S; Suchard Jeffrey; Tapia Antonio; Wiechmann Warren; Langdorf Mark I
abstract:
BACKGROUND
                        Recent surveys indicate that 48% of consumers actively use generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health-related inquiries. Despite widespread adoption and the potential to improve health care access, scant research examines the performance of AI chatbot responses regarding emergency care advice.
                
                                
                    OBJECTIVE
                        We assessed the quality of AI chatbot responses to common emergency care questions. We sought to determine qualitative differences in responses from 4 free-access AI chatbots, for 10 different serious and benign emergency conditions.
                
                                
                    METHODS
                        We created 10 emergency care questions that we fed into the free-access versions of ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI), Google Bard, Bing AI Chat (Microsoft), and Claude AI (Anthropic) on November 26, 2023. Each response was graded by 5 board-certified emergency medicine (EM) faculty for 8 domains of percentage accuracy, presence of dangerous information, factual accuracy, clarity, completeness, understandability, source reliability, and source relevancy. We determined the correct, complete response to the 10 questions from reputable and scholarly emergency medical references. These were compiled by an EM resident physician. For the readability of the chatbot responses, we used the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of each response from readability statistics embedded in Microsoft Word. Differences between chatbots were determined by the chi-square test.
                
                                
                    RESULTS
                        Each of the 4 chatbots’ responses to the 10 clinical questions were scored across 8 domains by 5 EM faculty, for 400 assessments for each chatbot. Together, the 4 chatbots had the best performance in clarity and understandability (both 85%), intermediate performance in accuracy and completeness (both 50%), and poor performance (10%) for source relevance and reliability (mostly unreported). Chatbots contained dangerous information in 5% to 35% of responses, with no statistical difference between chatbots on this metric (<i>P</i>=.24). ChatGPT, Google Bard, and Claud AI had similar performances across 6 out of 8 domains. Only Bing AI performed better with more identified or relevant sources (40%; the others had 0%-10%). Flesch-Kincaid Reading level was 7.7-8.9 grade for all chatbots, except ChatGPT at 10.8, which were all too advanced for average emergency patients. Responses included both dangerous (eg, starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation with no pulse check) and generally inappropriate advice (eg, loosening the collar to improve breathing without evidence of airway compromise).
                
                                
                    CONCLUSIONS
                        AI chatbots, though ubiquitous, have significant deficiencies in EM patient advice, despite relatively consistent performance. Information for when to seek urgent or emergent care is frequently incomplete and inaccurate, and patients may be unaware of misinformation. Sources are not generally provided. Patients who use AI to guide health care decisions assume potential risks. AI chatbots for health should be subject to further research, refinement, and regulation. We strongly recommend proper medical consultation to prevent potential adverse outcomes.
                
                                
                    CLINICALTRIAL

title: The Triple Illusion Architecture: An Ontological Analysis of Systematic Knowledge Gaps in Large Language Model Interactions
authors: Nguyen Kevin
journal: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable linguistic fluency, leading to widespread anthropomorphization and misattribution of cognitive capabilities. We present the first systematic ontological analysis revealing a Triple Illusion Architecture in human-LLM interactions: Layer I illusions emerge from triple approximation errors (embedding, prediction, and reference frame gaps), Layer II illusions arise from human cognitive biases attributing consciousness to statistical processing, and Layer III illusions stem from false beliefs about AI's access to complete human knowledge. Our Reference Frame Gap Theory demonstrates that training data systematically excludes the knowledge of innovative thinkers, cultural outliers, and domain experts, creating an insurmountable Genius Gap where LLMs fail precisely when interacting with individuals capable of advancing human understanding. Drawing on Searle's Chinese Room argument and recent empirical studies, we prove that hallucination is not an engineering problem but an epistemological inevitability of systems approximating meaning through incomplete statistical patterns. This framework explains why LLM capabilities are systematically overestimated and reveals a fundamental bias toward intellectual mediocrity in AI-human collaboration.

title: Large language model-based evaluation of the impact of gender in medical research
authors: Yao Michael S.
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Background
                  Gender disparities in academic medicine have been previously reported, but prior bibliometric studies have been limited by small sample sizes and reliance on manual gender annotation methods. These bottlenecks constrain previous analyses to only a small subset of clinical literature. To assess gender-based differences in authorship trends, research impact, and scholarly output over time in clinical research at scale, we hypothesized that large language models (LLMs) can be an effective tool to facilitate systematic bibliometric analysis of academic research trends.
                
                
                  Methods
                  We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional bibliometric study evaluating manuscripts published between January 2015 and September 2025 across over 1,000 PubMed-indexed academic medical journals. Over 1 million manuscripts, written by more than 10 million authors across 13 medical specialties, were analyzed. To enable this large-scale study, the genders of manuscript authors were annotated using a scalable LLM-based pipeline compatible with consumer-grade hardware.
                
                
                  Results
                  We found that the proportion of female principal investigators has increased over time across different medical subspecialties. However, studies led by male authors tended to be published in higher-impact journals and cited more frequently than those led by female authors. We also observed that researchers of the same gender tended to work together when compared to colleagues of the opposite gender.
                
                
                  Conclusions
                  While our findings revealed persistent gender-based differences in authorship trends, citation practices, and journal placement, we also observed ongoing, meaningful progress in female representation within academic medical research over time. Our results suggest that LLMs can be a powerful tool to scalably and periodically track this continued progress in future academic medical research.
                
                
                  Plain Language Summary
                  Academic research is important to advance the field and practice of medicine. To obtain an accurate picture of the differences in medical research and impact between male and female researchers, we leveraged large language models (LLMs) to identify author genders for over one million medical research papers published between 2015 and 2025. We found that the number of women serving as lead researchers has increased over time across many medical specialties. However, important gaps in achieving gender equality in medical research remain. Our study ultimately helps demonstrate that LLMs can help us monitor gender-based trends in academic research in the future.

title: An Experimental Analysis of BLEU Score Validity Across Large Language Model Use Cases
authors: Alfaro Pizana Ana Elvira
abstract: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is the dominant automatic evaluation metric in natural language generation, yet its validity is frequently assumed rather than demonstrated across the diverse use cases enabled by large language models (LLMs). We design and execute a controlled experiment across six representative LLM use cases-machine translation, data-to-text generation, code comment generation, summarisation, open-domain dialogue, and creative writing-using synthetic oracle data with known ground-truth quality scores. We prove formally that BLEU is a statistically valid quality proxy if and only if the valid output space is well-approximated by an ε-ball around the reference in meaning space, and we show empirically that this condition holds for near-deterministic tasks (Spearman ρ = 0.938 for MT) but collapses for high-entropy tasks (dialogue ρ = 0.110, p = 0.12; summarisation ρ =-0.069, p = 0.33). We demonstrate metric inversion-where BLEU ranks a high-quality output 4.9× lower than a worse output-in creative writing and dialogue. A t-test comparing mean Spearman correlations of valid versus invalid use cases yields t = 4.07, p = 0.015. We conclude with a practical decision table and recommendations grounded in the metric-space geometry developed throughout.

title: Efficacy Of Chatgpt-4 in Oral Hygiene Counseling: Evaluation of Information Accuracy and Repeatability
authors: Erimli Gözde; Kılıç Duygu; Yıldırım Yeşim Ayhan
journal: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract:
Abstract
                Background
 Oral hygiene habits play a crucial role in preventing periodontal diseases. Patients often require expert guidance to obtain personal dental tools and oral health information.  This study aims to evaluate the performance of ChatGPT-4 in providing high-quality information on oral hygiene habits.
Methods
 Thirty open-ended questions were prepared and categorized under three groups related to maintaining periodontal health. In March 2024, each question was asked of ChatGPT 30 times, resulting in 900 responses. The responses obtained were independently evaluated by experts using a 3-point Likert scale. Three reference sources were used during the question preparation and response evaluation phases. The expert scores' absolute (n) and relative frequency (%) were calculated. Accuracy was assessed using the Wald binomial method, while accuracy across groups was evaluated using the Fisher-Freeman-Halton test. The Benchmark scale assessment was used to determine repeatability and consistency. The confidence interval was set at 95%. Data were analyzed using IBM® SPSS® and R software.
Results
 ChatGPT-4’s accuracy rate in answering the questions was 81.4%. The confidence interval ranged between 78.8% and 83.9%.  ChatGPT-4 provided a higher accuracy rate (88.5%) for questions in the "Oral Antimicrobials and Toothpaste" group compared to other groups. Repeatability ranged between "Almost Perfect" and "Substantial."
Conclusions
 ChatGPT-4 could be a valuable virtual assistant integrated into clinics, providing expert-level information on oral hygiene habits for patients and healthcare professionals.

title: Automated Clinical Calculations in Critical Care and Perioperative Medicine: Accuracy Assessment of Clinician-Facing Large Language Models
authors: Rozman Robert C.; Barr Austin A.; Doyle Marcus A.; West Nicholas; Görges Matthias

title: High Average Accuracy Coexists with Substantial Between-Setting Variability: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Large Language Models for Data Extraction in Evidence Synthesis
authors: Bersot Carlos Darcy Alves
journal: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for data extraction in systematic reviews, but reported performance varies across extraction tasks, models, domains, reference standards, and definitions of correctness. We systematically reviewed empirical studies of automated or AI-assisted data extraction for evidence synthesis and performed an estimand-driven meta-analysis of uncorrected LLM extraction against human or otherwise validated reference standards. Forty-six reports representing 45 independent study units were included in the systematic review. Eight independent studies contributed 10 model-level estimates and 29,643 item-level evaluations to the broad primary quantitative synthesis. Proportions were analyzed on the logit scale using a multilevel random-effects model with model-level estimates nested within study and cluster-robust inference. Pooled item-level accuracy was 86.4% (cluster-robust 95% CI, 62.6%–96.0%), with generalized I² of 99.6% and a model-based 95% prediction interval of 19.2%–99.4%, indicating marked between-setting variability. In a construct-restricted sensitivity analysis excluding an open-ended, recall-intensive extraction setting, seven studies contributed nine model-level estimates and 29,343 item-level evaluations; pooled accuracy was 91.2% (95% CI, 83.1%–95.6%) and the prediction interval narrowed to 66.7%–98.2%. Leave-one-study-out analyses showed that omission of individual studies other than this methodologically distinct setting had comparatively limited influence on the pooled mean, whereas heterogeneity remained substantial. Across the broader evidence base, performance varied according to extraction task, data type, workflow design, and definition of correctness. These findings indicate that average LLM extraction accuracy can be high, but performance cannot be assumed to generalize across evidence-synthesis settings. Task-specific validation and human verification remain important, particularly for ambiguous, missing, derived, numerical, or otherwise consequential information

title: Large Language Models for Clinical Laboratory Reference-Range Classification: Evaluation Study of Model Scale, Prompt Language, and Contextual Information (Preprint)
authors: Shinohara Emiko; Kawazoe Yoshimasa
abstract:
BACKGROUND
                  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for clinical information processing and reasoning, where numerical values must often be interpreted relative to explicit thresholds or reference ranges. Although classifying laboratory values as low, within range, or high is deterministic when the reference range is given, numerical comparison can constitute a basic component of more complex clinical reasoning. Previous studies have evaluated the overall accuracy of such tasks, but less is known about where errors occur relative to decision boundaries and how model scale, prompt formulation, and task-irrelevant clinical context affect performance.
                
                
                  OBJECTIVE
                  This study aimed to characterize LLM performance in clinical laboratory reference-range classification as a function of model scale, measurement position relative to reference-range boundaries, Japanese versus English prompt formulations, and the inclusion of laboratory test names and units.
                
                
                  METHODS
                  Of the 43 clinical laboratory items initially considered, 40 met the prespecified criterion and were included in the analysis. We synthetically generated 6429 measurements from the publicly available reference ranges of these 40 items, with LOW, IN, and HIGH values systematically positioned relative to the lower and upper boundaries. We evaluated 10 open LLMs from the Qwen3 (0.6B-32B) and Gemma 4 families (E2B-31B) under 8 prompt conditions combining Japanese or English prompts with the presence or absence of test names and units. Thinking mode was disabled. Predictions were determined from the first-step next-token probabilities of candidate LOW, IN, and HIGH tokens, and item-and-label macro accuracy was the primary outcome. No human participants or patient data were used; ethics approval was not required.
                
                
                  RESULTS
                  Performance increased substantially with model scale but differed between model families. Qwen3 macro accuracy was 0.350 at 0.6B, 0.397 at 1.7B, 0.863 at 4B, and 0.966-0.976 at 8B-32B. Gemma accuracy increased from 0.865 at E2B and 0.946 at E4B to 0.995 at 12B and 0.998 at 31B. Qwen models retained localized errors near the upper reference-range boundary even at larger scales; in Qwen3-32B, the mean IN-versus-HIGH log-probability difference crossed zero at a normalized position of approximately 0.96, before the stated upper boundary of 1.0. In contrast, position-dependent errors largely disappeared in Gemma 12B and 31B. Adding test names or units did not consistently improve performance and significantly reduced accuracy in several models (Holm-adjusted P<.05), with particularly pronounced effects in Gemma E2B and E4B. Differences between Japanese and English prompt conditions varied by model and label, with no consistently superior prompt language.
                
                
                  CONCLUSIONS
                  LLM reference-range classification cannot be fully characterized by overall accuracy or model scale alone. Error localization near numerical boundaries and sensitivity to additional clinical context differed substantially across model families and sizes. Controlled evaluation of such basic numerical operations may complement task-level benchmarks when assessing LLMs for more complex clinical information processing and reasoning.

title: Citation Fabrication and Accuracy in AI-Generated Psychiatric Research: A Comparative Evaluation of Four Contemporary Large Language Models
authors: Linardon Jake; Anderson Cleo; Bolger Tayarna; Liu Claudia; Soliman Olivia Marie; McClure Zoe
abstract: Objectives. LLMs are increasingly used to support academic writing, but their tendency to hallucinate citations raises concerns about the integrity of AI-assisted scholarly work. This study provides a timely snapshot of citation reliability in LLM-generated academic reviews by testing whether citation fabrication and accuracy differ across four LLMs and review topic specificity. Method. ChatGPT-5.4 Plus, ChatGPT-5.3 Free, Gemini-3, and Claude Sonnet-4.6 were tasked with generating 16 literature reviews on mental health, divided into general topics (broad areas with substantial evidence bases) and specialised topics (narrower areas with smaller evidence bases). Results. Only 6.1% of the 825 LLM-generated citations were fabricated, with fabrication absent for ChatGPT-5.4 Plus (0%), very low for Claude Sonnet-4.6 (0.5%) and ChatGPT-5.3 Free (5.5%), and highest for Google Gemini-3 (20.2%). A similar model-level pattern emerged for citation accuracy (real citations containing no bibliographic errors). Review topic specificity was not associated with citation fabrication or accuracy. Conclusion. Findings suggest possible improvements in citation reliability relative to estimates from prior studies testing older model iterations, while also showing that current performance is strongly model-dependent. These findings highlight the need for rigorous human verification of LLM-generated references and stronger safeguards to protect research integrity as LLMs are integrated into research.

title: Comparative Analysis of Rule Based Symbolic Logic and a Large Language Model in Sanskrit Morphological Analysis
authors: Chaurasia Khyati
journal: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract:
Abstract
                Sanskrit morphology provides a setting for comparing explicit suffix rules and language-model predictions under changes in word order. This exploratory study evaluates a Python suffix classifier and supplied Gemini prediction files for 100 Bhagavad Gita entries representing 98 distinct verse identifiers. The corpus contains 614 split-token occurrences and 280 selective reference annotations. Natural and scrambled inputs preserve the same token multisets. A scoring audit identified repeated matching and unconditional credit for ambiguous outputs in the original symbolic evaluator. Using one-to-one annotation matching and candidate-set membership, the unchanged symbolic classifier achieved compatibility on 228/280 annotations (81.43%) in each order. The supplied natural and scrambled Gemini CSVs each achieved 242/280 compatible predictions (86.43%), after resolving one scrambled-token transcription mismatch by its input position. Only two of 614 paired Gemini classifications changed; neither affected the annotated score. The comparison shows no decrease in compatibility under scrambling and documents stable compatibility in this recorded comparison, alongside limitations from selective annotations, candidate ambiguity, and incomplete model metadata. The results describe robustness of these outputs under the supplied permutations rather than general word-order invariance or full morphological parsing accuracy.

title: Half of alcohol, drug, and self-harm presentations cannot be identified in coded emergency department data: a diagnostic accuracy study of a large language model
authors: Humphries Chris; Brett Jonathan; Gruber Franz; James Edward; McKendrick Tuesday I; McNairn Kimberley C; Miell Anna; O’Brien Rachel; Rahman Fahrurrozi; Schölin Lisa; Stewart Morven; Casey Arlene
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Objective
                  To measure the accuracy of clinical coding, clinician review, and a locally deployed large language model (LLM) in identifying alcohol, drug, and self-harm involvement in emergency department (ED) attendances, and quantify prevalence.
                
                
                  Design
                  Two-phase diagnostic accuracy study. In a validation week, the identification strategies were assessed against a conflict-adjudicated reference standard (n=2,256); the LLM was then applied to n=105,096 annual attendances at the same site.
                
                
                  Setting
                  UK Type 1 Emergency Department treating patients ≥16yrs.
                
                
                  Main outcome measures
                  Prevalence quantification compared with the reference standard; sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy of each strategy; monthly identification rates and adjusted annual prevalence.
                
                
                  Results
                  The reference standard identified 12.1% of attendances as involving alcohol, drugs, or self-harm (coding 6.0%; clinician 10.0%, LLM 15.6%). LLM balanced accuracy matched or outperformed clinician review in all three domains (alcohol 0.942 v 0.930, p=0.635; drug 0.959 v 0.791, p<0.001; self-harm 0.982 v 0.908, p=0.004). Coding recorded 1.07 domains per identified patient against 1.32 in the reference standard. Adjusted annual prevalence corresponded to 12,890 domain involvements per year not identifiable in coded data. Subdomain classification found at least 81.6% of self-harm attendances required medical assessment for injury or overdose before psychiatric review.
                
                
                  Conclusions
                  Clinical coding identified fewer than half of presentations involving alcohol, drugs, and self-harm and rarely captured co-occurring domains; under-recording was present across a full year. A locally deployed LLM generated more complete structured data from existing clinical text within NHS infrastructure, at a scale which is not feasible for manual review.
                
                
                  What is already known on this topic
                  
                    
                      Coded emergency department data underpin national surveillance, commissioning, research, and service planning, but the size and direction of their error for specific conditions have not been measured against a validated reference standard in an unselected population.
                    
                  
                
                
                  What this study adds
                  
                    
                      In a UK emergency department, clinical coding identified 6.0% of attendances as involving alcohol, drugs, or self-harm against an adjudicated reference-standard prevalence of 12.1%.
                    
                    
                      In blinded head-to-head comparison, a locally deployed, open-source large language model achieved similar or higher balanced accuracy than clinician review. Applied to 105,096 attendances over 12 months, it identified 14.3% of attendances against 4.1% by coding, in every month of the year.
                    
                  
                
                
                  How this study might affect research, practice, or policy
                  
                    
                      Prevalence estimates and service planning based on coded emergency department data are likely to understate both the burden and the co-occurrence of these conditions. The majority (81.6%) of classified self-harm presentations required medical assessment for injury or overdose; only 18.4% did not, a figure directly relevant to mental health emergency-care streaming. Locally deployed open-source language models offer a scalable, governance-compatible method for identifying these presentations from existing free text.

title: OHCA-EXTRACT: Evaluating the Accuracy of a Large Language Model Pipeline for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Case Identification and Utstein Variable Extraction
authors: Shekhar Aditya C; Apakama Donald; Saharan Aryan; Petrozzo Kevin; Jiang Joy; Zebrowski Alexis; Buckler David; Huebinger Ryan; Abella Benjamin S; Richardson Lynne D; Nadkarni Girish N; Abbott Ethan E
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Background
                  Manual identification and abstraction of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) cases and Utstein template variables from electronic health records is resource-intensive and limits scalable measurement for observational research and registry participation. We evaluated a large language model (LLM)–assisted pipeline to identify true OHCA encounters within an ICD-coded emergency department (ED) cohort and to also extract a limited set of Utstein variables from unstructured documentation, with iterative pipeline refinement and final performance evaluation conducted on the same validation cohort.
                
                
                  Methods
                  We conducted a study of ICD-flagged OHCA encounters within a large urban academic health system (2015–2024). A two-module pipeline was developed that included an identification module and a variable-extraction module. The pipeline was evaluated against independent manual chart abstraction on a validation sample (n = 176) with physician adjudication. The identification module performed binary OHCA classification along with etiology classification. The variable-extraction module extracted five Utstein variables: witnessed status, EMS defibrillation, first recorded rhythm, arrest location, and bystander response. We calculated sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and F1 scores (Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs) using the manual chart abstraction as the reference gold standard.
                
                
                  Results
                  Of 176 processed encounters, 152 had complete gold-standard classification and were included in identification analyses (OHCA prevalence 81.6%; n = 124 true OHCA, n = 28 non-OHCA). The identification module achieved an accuracy of 0.91 (95% CI 0.85–0.95), sensitivity 0.94 (0.89–0.98), specificity 0.75 (0.55–0.89), PPV 0.94 (0.89–0.98), NPV 0.75 (0.55–0.89), and F1 0.94, compared with accuracy 0.82 for a prevalence-only baseline. Variable-level accuracy ranged from 0.63 to 0.75 (Kappa range 0.31–0.51) across the five extracted Utstein variables, with bystander response showing the lowest agreement (accuracy 0.63, Kappa = 0.31).
                
                
                  Conclusions
                  Within-sample performance estimates indicate that this LLM pipeline can identify true OHCA encounters within an ICD-flagged ED cohort with accuracy and PPV above an administrative-coding baseline. Variable-level extraction accuracy ranged from fair to moderate across the five evaluated Utstein variables, indicating that further methodological development is required before automated extraction is feasible. With external validation and integration with targeted human verification, this approach may support human-augmented workflows using LLMs, however independent external validation is required before our findings can be generalized.

title: Evaluation of the Performance of Generative AI Large Language Models ChatGPT, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing Chat in Supporting Evidence-Based Dentistry: Comparative Mixed Methods Study (Preprint)
authors: Giannakopoulos Kostis; Kavadella Argyro; Aaqel Salim Anas; Stamatopoulos Vassilis; Kaklamanos Eleftherios G
abstract:
BACKGROUND
                        The increasing application of generative artificial intelligence large language models (LLMs) in various fields, including dentistry, raises questions about their accuracy.
                
                                
                    OBJECTIVE
                        This study aims to comparatively evaluate the answers provided by 4 LLMs, namely Bard (Google LLC), ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI), and Bing Chat (Microsoft Corp), to clinically relevant questions from the field of dentistry.
                
                                
                    METHODS
                        The LLMs were queried with 20 open-type, clinical dentistry–related questions from different disciplines, developed by the respective faculty of the School of Dentistry, European University Cyprus. The LLMs’ answers were graded 0 (minimum) to 10 (maximum) points against strong, traditionally collected scientific evidence, such as guidelines and consensus statements, using a rubric, as if they were examination questions posed to students, by 2 experienced faculty members. The scores were statistically compared to identify the best-performing model using the Friedman and Wilcoxon tests. Moreover, the evaluators were asked to provide a qualitative evaluation of the comprehensiveness, scientific accuracy, clarity, and relevance of the LLMs’ answers.
                
                                
                    RESULTS
                        Overall, no statistically significant difference was detected between the scores given by the 2 evaluators; therefore, an average score was computed for every LLM. Although ChatGPT-4 statistically outperformed ChatGPT-3.5 (<i>P</i>=.008), Bing Chat (<i>P</i>=.049), and Bard (<i>P</i>=.045), all models occasionally exhibited inaccuracies, generality, outdated content, and a lack of source references. The evaluators noted instances where the LLMs delivered irrelevant information, vague answers, or information that was not fully accurate.
                
                                
                    CONCLUSIONS
                        This study demonstrates that although LLMs hold promising potential as an aid in the implementation of evidence-based dentistry, their current limitations can lead to potentially harmful health care decisions if not used judiciously. Therefore, these tools should not replace the dentist’s critical thinking and in-depth understanding of the subject matter. Further research, clinical validation, and model improvements are necessary for these tools to be fully integrated into dental practice. Dental practitioners must be aware of the limitations of LLMs, as their imprudent use could potentially impact patient care. Regulatory measures should be established to oversee the use of these evolving technologies.
                
                                
                    CLINICALTRIAL

title: A Fully Local Offline Framework for Enterprise Document Intelligence Using Retrieval-Based Large Language Model Grounding
authors: Rawat Anand; Kumar Sanjeev
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as an effective paradigm for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge, thereby reducing hallucinations and improving factual consistency in document-centric question answering. However, most practical RAG deployments rely on cloud-hosted Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), remote vector stores, or proprietary inference services, raising privacy, sovereignty, latency, and cost concerns for government, defense, finance, healthcare, and industrial organizations. This paper presents a fully local offline RAG framework that transforms Portable Document Format (PDF) rulebooks and enterprise documents into a secure on-premise conversational intelligence system without requiring external APIs or cloud connectivity.The proposed framework integrates page-wise PDF ingestion using PyMuPDF, document normalization, metadata-aware semantic chunking, local embedding generation using nomic-embed-text, Chroma vector database indexing, and answer synthesis through Ollama-hosted LLMs, including the Meta Llama 3 8-billion-parameter model and the Qwen 2.5 14-billion-parameter model. Structured metadata extraction, source-grounded citation generation, low-memory model routing, and an interactive Streamlit interface further support practical deployment. A hybrid retrieval strategy combining dense semantic similarity with metadata constraints is introduced to improve retrieval precision for rule-based documents.A real-world case study using the General Financial Rules (GFR 2017) demonstrates the effectiveness of the framework for procurement and compliance question answering. Experimental results show competitive retrieval quality, low hallucination rates, acceptable response latency, and modest memory requirements on consumer-grade hardware while preserving data confidentiality and eliminating recurring API costs. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for privacy-preserving enterprise document intelligence and sovereign Artificial Intelligence (AI) deployment.

title: Silent numerical failures in large language model–generated pharmacokinetic simulation code: a benchmark against target-controlled infusion validation criteria using the Marsh propofol model
authors: Omote Masahito
abstract:
Abstract
                
                  Background
                  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by clinicians to generate executable code for pharmacokinetic (PK) simulation. Whether such code meets the accuracy standards of target-controlled infusion systems has not been systematically evaluated.
                
                
                  Methods
                  Five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok) were prompted to generate Python code for the Marsh three-compartment propofol model under a standardized 120-minute bolus-plus-infusion regimen. Each LLM was tested in two phases: Phase 1, integrator free; Phase 2, fourth-order Runge–Kutta with 1-second step size mandated. Twenty runs per LLM per phase were collected (n = 200). Plasma concentrations were compared against a triple-validated reference using median prediction error (MDPE), median absolute prediction error (MDAPE), and Wobble. Runs were classified as Class A (MDAPE < 1 %), B (1–30 %), C (≥ 30 %), or D (failed).
                
                
                  Results
                  
                    All 200 scripts were invokable and created a CSV file; 199/200 (99.5 %, 95 % CI 97.1–99.9 %) produced a valid time–concentration series. The remaining script (Gemini Phase 2 run 18) aborted during row formatting with
                    ValueError
                    and left a header-only CSV. Median MDAPE per LLM × phase ranged 0.0043–0.020 %, with 195/200 runs (97.5 %, 95 % CI 94.3–98.9 %) achieving Class A. Five runs (2.5 %, 95 % CI 1.1–5.7 %) were non-excellent or structurally defective: three were Class C due to time-scale/unit-handling errors (one DeepSeek run with a 6-second effective Euler step from a minute-as-second declaration, two Grok runs with min⁻¹ rate constants applied per second), one was Class D (the empty-CSV failure above), and one was Class B but reflected a duplicated-bolus implementation error rather than a benign numerical deviation. Kruskal–Wallis testing showed significant inter-LLM heterogeneity across all metrics and phases (all omnibus p < 0.01). Strict compliance with Phase 2 directives was 98 % (98/100 runs; 95 % CI 93.1–99.5 %); lenient compliance accepting RK4-adaptive implementations as a superset was 100 % (100/100 runs; 95 % CI 96.3–100 %). Yet all three numerically divergent Phase 2 runs occurred under nominally compliant RK4/dt = 1 s configurations; the fourth non-Class-A Phase 2 outcome was a formatting failure that produced no usable trajectory.
                  
                
                
                  Conclusion
                  LLMs generate numerically accurate Marsh-model code in most runs but silently diverge in a clinically non-negligible minority. The Marsh model — the simplest fixed-parameter three-compartment propofol model — functioned here as a positive control: even so, three distinct classes of structural bug (unit/time-scale mismatch, duplicated-bolus event handling, malformed f-string formatting) slipped past apparent execution success. Two additional Phase 2 runs used an RK4-adaptive variant rather than classical RK4 and are therefore better interpreted as strict prompt non-compliance than as numerical failure. Prompt-level method specification substantially reduced algorithm-selection errors but did not eliminate unit or structural bugs. LLM-generated pharmacokinetic code requires reference-based validation before any safety-relevant use.

title: Mapping the Immediate Trajectory of Retinal Disease Research: A Large Language Model-Assisted Bibliometric Analysis
authors: Su Zheng; Li Tinsley
journal: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract:
Abstract
                Retinal diseases are major causes of global blindness, with emerging treatments and artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly reshaping care. Conventional bibliometrics relying on lifetime citations suffer from temporal bias, often failing to capture immediate research frontiers. We aimed to map the immediate trajectory of high-impact retinal disease research by comparing influential literature from 2023 and 2024. We performed a retrospective, large language model (LLM)–assisted bibliometric analysis of 100 highly cited OpenAlex articles (50 per year), ranked by 18-month citation impact. LLMs verified topical relevance, extracted concepts, and normalized them into 89 parent themes and 874 canonical topics. Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic eye disease remained the dominant parent theme (normalized frequency 0.48 to 0.50), while retinal degenerative and inherited diseases and diabetes mellitus and its complications rose modestly (+0.06 and +0.04, respectively). Diabetic retinopathy grading increased (+0.10), whereas convolutional neural network (−0.22) and fundus imaging (−0.20) declined; large language models and genome-wide association study emerged (+0.06 each). These findings indicate a shift from foundational imaging-based machine learning toward clinical diabetic retinopathy management, genomic studies, and deployed AI tools. A web app (https://pri.pepkio.com) supports data exploration.

title: Automated Phenotypic Characterisation In Rare Haematological Malignancies Using A Large Language Model-Based Framework: A Retrospective Diagnostic Accuracy Study
authors: Khan Muhammad Ali; Ayub Umair; Jajja Salman  Ayub; Anjum Muhammad  Umair; Warraich Kainat; Jain Prateek; Oberoi Japneet  Kaur; Al Abbas Mousab; Sadiq Muhammad  Hussnain; Sarfraz Muhammad  Uzair; Humayun Mohammad Abdullah; Huang Ziyi; Riaz Irbaz; Palmer Jeanne  M.
abstract: Background:&nbsp;Phenotyping rare haematological malignancies requires integrating dispersed electronic health record (EHR) data, making manual abstraction labour intensive. Using myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) as a use case, we evaluated a large language model (LLM) and rule-based framework for classification and risk stratification.<br><br>Methods:&nbsp;We conducted a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study across Mayo Clinic sites (USA). Patients with bone marrow biopsies were randomly sampled from ICD-9/10-coded cohorts for polycythaemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythaemia (ET), or myelofibrosis (MF). Cases met 2022 WHO criteria or had a definitive haematologist-documented diagnosis; controls met neither criterion. Two clinicians independently established the reference standard, with third-clinician adjudication. Prompts were developed in 60 patients, frozen, then tested in 450 (75 cases and 75 controls per disease). GPT-4 Turbo extracted variables from pathology reports and clinical notes; clinician-defined rules integrated structured laboratory data and applied WHO/ICC criteria and risk models. Outcomes were extraction accuracy, diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, and risk-category accuracy.<br><br>Findings:&nbsp;Chart review spanned May, 2023, to July, 2025. Of 450 test-set patients, 228 (50·7%) were male. All had pathology reports and structured laboratory data; 172 (38·2%) had clinical notes. Extraction accuracy was 99–100% in pathology reports and 96–100% in notes. Sensitivity was 100% (75/75; 95% CI 95·1–100·0) for each disease; specificity was 98·7% (74/75; 92·8–99·8) for PV and 100% (75/75; 95·1–100·0) for ET and MF. Risk-category accuracy was 100% (75/75; 95·1–100·0) for each disease.<br><br>Interpretation:&nbsp;Multisource LLM-assisted phenotyping could support MPN research workflows reliant on manual abstraction. External and prospective validation is needed before implementation.Funding&nbsp;None.

title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration
authors: Wang Ruo-Qian
abstract: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder–Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient—disappearing by fifteen evaluations—and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder–Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.

title: Evaluative Cultural Hallucination in Large Language Model Assessment of Tenor in Scenic Area Public Sign Translations
authors: Guo Qi; Yap Tengteng
journal: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract: This study investigates whether large language models overestimate the Tenor quality of culturally sensitive scenic-area public-sign translations. Drawing on House’s translation quality assessment framework, Tenor was operationalized as the pragmatic and socio-cultural appropriateness of English public signs. A corpus of 116 Chinese-English bilingual public signs from eight 4A/5A tourist attractions in Xuzhou, China, was evaluated by human experts and GPT-5.5 Thinking on the basis of the Chinese source text, the English translation, and relevant scenic-area contextual information, including attraction name, sign type, and thematic category. High-overestimation cases were defined as samples with an expert Tenor score of ≤2 and an LLM score of ≥4. Results showed that 56 samples, or 48.3% of the corpus, met this criterion, with religious and ritual signs showing the highest proportion of overestimation. Qualitative coding of the 56 LLM rationales identified four recurrent rationale patterns: formal-register overreliance, semantic recognizability substitution, generic reverence substitution, and omission-tolerant simplification. These findings suggest that LLMs may mistake surface formality, recognizable cultural references, general solemnity, or concise expression for Tenor appropriateness. The study frames this problem as evaluative cultural hallucination and highlights the need for expert-informed, culturally sensitive safeguards in LLM-assisted translation quality assessment.

title: Developing a large language model for a self-directed triage training program using artificial intelligence
authors: Uyanage Tharindu; Silva Suriyaarachchige Nishan; Uyanage Isuru
abstract:
Abstract
                
                Triaging is a crucial process within emergency departments (EDs), designed to prioritize patients based on the urgency of their condition. It relies heavily on both numerical vital parameters and descriptive triage notes. However, triage decisions are often influenced by local disease patterns, demographic variations, and institutional guidelines, making the process context-dependent. Despite this, existing triage training programs are largely generic and fail to represent the local uniqueness of clinical practice.
                This study proposes an Artificial Intelligence (AI) based approach to develop a hospital-specific triage prediction model using a Large Language Model (LLM) architecture. The AI model learns directly from local triage data, allowing it to simulate real-world triage decision-making patterns. The trained model will be integrated into a self-directed, scenario-based online triage training program hosted on a Moodle platform. The program aims to provide learners with AI-generated feedback, bridging the gap between conventional training and localized, data-driven education.
                
                
                  1. Introduction
                
                Emergency triage plays a pivotal role in ensuring timely patient care. It involves assessing the severity of a patient’s condition and assigning an appropriate triage category, typically ranging from Level 1 (resuscitation) to Level 5 (non-urgent) according to the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS). The accuracy and consistency of triage decisions are vital for optimizing patient outcomes and resource allocation in busy emergency settings.
                Traditional triage training programs rely on standardized case studies and manual instruction, which may not fully reflect the variations in regional disease prevalence, patient demographics, and institutional protocols. These differences can significantly influence how triage nurses interpret patient symptoms and vital signs. Consequently, healthcare professionals often require additional localized training to achieve optimal decision-making accuracy within their own clinical environments.
                Artificial Intelligence has demonstrated increasing potential in modeling complex clinical reasoning. By learning from real-world data, AI can emulate human decision-making and highlight underlying patterns that may not be evident through conventional rule-based systems. This study leverages machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to develop a predictive triage model capable of reproducing the decision logic specific to a single hospital. The model then serves as the foundation for an adaptive self-directed training platform.
                
                
                  2. Objectives
                
                
                  The primary objectives of this study were to:
                  
                    
                      Develop a machine learning–based triage prediction model using real hospital data that includes both vital signs and triage notes.
                    
                    
                      Evaluate and compare multiple algorithms to identify the model with the best accuracy and interpretability.
                    
                    
                      Integrate the model into a self-directed triage training platform that provides learners with real-time, AI-generated feedback and explanations.
                    
                    
                      Demonstrate how AI can support region-specific clinical education, bridging the gap between generalized and localized triage training.
                    
                  
                  3. Methods
                
                
                  3.1 Data Collection
                
                The dataset comprised three years of anonymized triage records collected from a metropolitan hospital in Victoria, Australia. Each record included structured numerical data such as blood pressure, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and temperature, and unstructured text data from triage notes that describe the patient’s presenting complaint and the nurse’s initial observations. All data were de-identified before analysis to ensure compliance with privacy and ethical standards.
                
                
                  3.2 Data Preprocessing
                
                Data preprocessing involved cleaning and standardizing numerical features, managing missing values, and normalizing outlier ranges. The free-text triage notes were processed using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, and the creation of Word2Vec embeddings to transform clinical text into numerical representations that capture semantic meaning.
                
                
                  3.3 Model Development
                
                Eight machine learning and deep learning models were developed and evaluated for triage level prediction. These models incorporated both structured and unstructured clinical inputs, combining vital parameters (e.g., blood pressure, oxygen saturation, heart rate) with triage notes describing the patient’s presenting complaint and initial nurse observations.
                
                
                  The following models were implemented and tested:
                  
                    
                      Logistic Regression
                    
                    
                      Random Forest
                    
                    
                      FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with GloVe embeddings
                    
                    
                      FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with BioBERT embeddings
                    
                    
                      FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with BERT embeddings
                    
                    
                      FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with GPT-2 embeddings
                    
                    
                      Voting model combining Logistic Regression and Random Forest predictions
                    
                    
                      Voting model combining Gradient Boosting and Random Forest predictions
                    
                  
                  The deep learning models utilized pre-trained word embeddings (GloVe, BioBERT, BERT, and GPT-2) to extract semantic and contextual information from the triage notes, enhancing the model’s ability to interpret complex clinical language.
                
                
                To ensure transparency and clinical interpretability, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques were applied using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP analysis quantified the relative contribution of each input feature, including vital signs and key terms within triage notes, to the model’s final prediction. This process enabled visualization of how specific clinical variables influenced triage decisions and confirmed that the model’s reasoning aligned with expert clinical judgment.
                
                The combination of high predictive accuracy and explainability made the Random Forest + SHAP pipeline the most suitable candidate for integration into the self-directed triage training platform, ensuring both performance and interpretability for real-world educational use.
                
                
                  3.4 Model Evaluation
                
                The models were validated using stratified sampling and evaluated based on precision, recall, and F1-score metrics to ensure balanced performance across all triage levels.
                
                To ensure clinical reliability, a real-world validation framework was designed in collaboration with three official triage officers from the hospital. Together, we developed a structured test framework consisting of 10 anonymized triage cases that represented a range of clinical scenarios and triage levels. The officers independently reviewed these cases, and their assessments were used as the reference standard for validating model predictions.
                
                
                  4. Results and Analysis
                
                The Random Forest model demonstrated the best performance among all algorithms tested, achieving the following results:
                
                
                  The Random Forest model achieved:
                  
                    
                      
                        F1-score:
                        0.85
                      
                    
                    
                      
                        Overall accuracy:
                        87 %
                      
                    
                    
                      
                        Category 2 accuracy:
                        82 %
                      
                    
                    
                      
                        Category 1 accuracy:
                        64 %
                      
                    
                  
                  The lower performance for Category 1 cases reflects their rarity and complexity, suggesting that additional high-acuity data could further enhance accuracy.
                
                
                The findings indicate that AI can effectively learn the decision-making patterns underlying clinical triage. 
                
                  Real-world testing confirmed the model’s reliability in replicating hospital-specific triage behavior. Importantly, this result supports the broader hypothesis that
                  each hospital can train its own triage model
                  using local data, thereby preserving the individuality of its patient population and clinical workflows.
                
                
                
                  5. Integration into a Self-directed Training Platform
                
                Building on these results, the study’s second phase involves developing a scenario-based self-learning platform hosted on Moodle. In this platform, healthcare trainees will be presented with realistic triage cases derived from the dataset. After selecting an appropriate triage level, their decision will be compared with the AI model’s predicted “ideal” triage level and explanation.
                
                
                  The system provides immediate feedback that includes:
                  
                    
                      A rationale generated by the AI model, describing which clinical features influenced the decision.
                    
                    
                      Comparison with expert-validated triage categories.
                    
                    
                      Progress tracking and adaptive difficulty adjustment to personalize learning.
                    
                  
                  This approach offers a scalable and data-driven solution for ongoing triage education, particularly in resource-constrained environments where access to in-person training may be limited.
                
                
                
                  6. Discussion
                
                The study demonstrates that AI can replicate and explain hospital-specific triage patterns with a satisfactory level of accuracy. By combining vital parameters and narrative triage notes, the model bridges quantitative and qualitative aspects of clinical reasoning. Unlike static rule-based systems, the AI model learns dynamically from historical data, ensuring that it reflects real local practices.
                
                
                  From an educational perspective, integrating such models into training systems promotes self-directed learning, enabling healthcare professionals to independently practice and refine their clinical judgment. Moreover, explainable AI (XAI) methods, such as feature importance and SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), can further enhance learner understanding by showing
                  why
                  the model prioritized specific features.
                
                
                This framework can be adapted for different hospitals and regions worldwide. Each institution could train its own localized AI model using its internal triage data while maintaining privacy and security through anonymization. As more datasets are incorporated, these models could form the basis for national or regional triage training standards that balance consistency with contextual relevance.
                
                
                  7. Limitations
                
                
                  While the results are promising, several limitations must be acknowledged:
                  
                    
                      The dataset was limited to a single metropolitan hospital, which may restrict generalizability.
                    
                    
                      Category 1 (critical) cases were underrepresented, affecting accuracy for high-acuity predictions.
                    
                    
                      The model has not yet been deployed in a live training environment; educational impact will be evaluated in the next phase.
                    
                    
                      Natural language variations and abbreviations in triage notes can introduce interpretation challenges, which future iterations may address using larger LLM architectures or domain-specific embeddings.
                    
                  
                
                
                  8. Future Work
                
                
                  The next phase of research will involve:
                  
                    
                      Deploying the Moodle-based system for pilot testing among triage trainees.
                    
                    
                      Collecting user feedback to evaluate the educational effectiveness of AI-generated feedback.
                    
                    
                      Expanding the dataset to include additional hospitals to assess cross-institutional adaptability.
                    
                    
                      Integrating Explainable AI techniques (e.g., SHAP, LIME) to improve transparency and learner engagement.
                    
                  
                  Long-term, the goal is to develop a federated triage learning ecosystem where hospitals can train, validate, and share anonymized model weights, accelerating triage education globally while safeguarding patient data.
                
                
                
                  9. Conclusion
                
                This study successfully demonstrates that Artificial Intelligence can capture and reproduce the clinical reasoning patterns unique to individual hospitals. The Random Forest model achieved strong performance in predicting triage levels using combined vital parameters and triage notes. More importantly, the methodology can be adapted to any healthcare institution to generate its own hospital-specific triage model.
                By integrating this AI capability into a self-directed online learning environment, the project bridges the gap between generic training programs and context-aware clinical education. This represents a meaningful advancement toward personalized medical learning, where technology enhances, not replaces, human expertise.

title: Reconstructable, privacy-preserving provenance for FHIR-to-large language model clinical transactions: a protocol demonstration
authors: Mentey Satya  Venkata Ranga Janaki Sr
abstract: Background and Objectives: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems that consume electronic health record data and emit reviewer-facing summaries rarely preserve the inputs, transformations, model configuration, evidence, safeguards, and human disposition needed to reconstruct a transaction. Storing raw clinical payloads or hidden model reasoning in an immutable log to fill that gap is unsafe. This study asks whether one Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) to large language model (LLM) transaction can be reconstructed and integrity-checked without either. Methods: Curie Audit Plane separates protected clinical content from an append-only audit chain of typed events with content digests. A completed transaction root is placed in a one-leaf Merkle envelope and signed with Ed25519. Model output is constrained to structured rationale with evidence references, uncertainty, assumptions, and missing data; hidden chain-of-thought fields are rejected. A versioned harness reloads persisted records, runs a separate verifier module, applies 19 labeled mutations, ablates provenance classes, probes role-based access, and measures capture overhead against an identical unrecorded clinical workflow. Results: On synthetic FHIR Release 4 fixtures, reload-and-verify audit reconstruction completeness was 20 of 20 required fields. All 19 mutations produced a non-verified outcome (18 tampered, one incomplete), and 11 of 11 access probes matched their expected outcome. Complete capture added 103% mean latency (16.1 versus 8.6 ms; 95% interval 79–128%) and a 3.5-fold logical storage multiplier (7.2-fold allocated on disk). Conclusions: A data/proof split makes a bounded FHIR-to-LLM handoff reconstructable without placing raw protected health information or hidden reasoning in an immutable store. The contribution integrates known integrity and interoperability primitives into application software; overhead is substantial at single-transaction scale, and clinical or population-scale evaluation remains future work.

title: Right-Sized Distillation of an Edge Large Language Model for Live Multi-Protocol IoT Traffic Classification
authors: Koutras Dimitris; Paklatzis Vangelis; Kotzanikolaou Panayiotis
abstract: Low-power IoT deployments rely extensively on lightweight protocols such as the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) and Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT). While engineered for low overhead, this minimalism inherently strips away strong authentication and rate-limiting mechanisms, exposing a broad attack surface that includes CoAP amplification, MQTT Denial-of-Service (DoS), and TCP-based exploits. Existing intrusion detection systems largely depend on classical machine-learning classifiers; although accurate, these models only output opaque class indices. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide human-readable rationales and actionable mitigation strategies, yet their large memory footprint, high inference latency, and lack of protocol-specific awareness conventionally preclude their deployment on resource-constrained edge appliances. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel closed-loop pipeline for multi-protocol edge inference. Our methodology applies a right-sized teacher-distillation approach, combined with parameter-efficient Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning, to adapt a compact 2B effective-parameter student model from a moderately sized 4B teacher. We evaluate the proposed edge-deployable model against three large 27–31B reference models within a live, deterministic flow-window stream. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves an optimal operational trade-off, attaining 95% recall on CoAP amplification with only a 1.2% False-Alarm Rate (FAR). Furthermore, it achieves 100% recall for MQTT DoS, 82% for malformed MQTT, 100% for TCP scanning, and 86% for Telnet brute-force attacks. The results show that right-sized distillation produces an edge-feasible LLM that remains competitive with classical Machine Learning (ML), while additionally providing explanations and attack-specific mitigation guidance.

title: A Prompt-Based Tutorial for Large Language Model–Assisted Screening in Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
authors: Qiu Tongyu; Jiang Huangqi; Lin Tao
abstract: Title/abstract and full-text screening are among the most time-consuming stages of systematic reviews. Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT can assist in screening, but most prior evaluations focus only on abstract-level decisions and require coding or API access, limiting practical application. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a structured, prompt-based approach that enables LLMs to perform both abstract and full-text screening without programming or API integration. Using datasets from two completed meta-analyses, we implemented a stepwise training framework involving comprehension checks, criterion-specific feedback, and iterative prompt refinement. Study 1 optimized technical parameters, including file format and batch size, using 1,000 abstracts and 50 full texts from a completed meta-analysis. Study 2 validated the approach in an independent dataset on teletherapy for depression (1,321 abstracts, 82 full texts). Human reviewers’ decisions served as the reference standard, and sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were the primary outcomes. In Study 1, the LLM achieved 98.0% sensitivity and 80.6% specificity at abstract screening, with optimal performance using batches of 50 abstracts in plain-text format.
